description: Este grupo va a estar conformado por 5 personas, para resolver el challenge de crear un juego.
summary: Orbital is a browser-based 3D game where players design and fly real-style NASA science missions, from Earth orbit to the Moon, with Mars chapters planned. Players assemble a rocket stage by stage, launch it with keyboard controls, perform a gravity turn and reach orbit using simplified but realistic physics: gravity, atmosphere, heating, Max-Q, staging, maneuver nodes and Earth–Moon patched conics. Once in space, they operate instruments inspired by Landsat, SWOT and LRO to answer real scientific questions. They track surface water changes on Earth, map lunar slopes with a laser altimeter, and drive a rover to measure lunar surface temperature. Data only counts once it is transmitted to a ground station within range and power limits. A guided tutorial teaches Δv, apoapsis, periapsis, TWR and SAS step by step, and failing never costs progress. Each mission ends with a report that separates simulated measurements from what NASA actually published. Orbital makes orbital mechanics and mission science accessible, hands-on and bilingual (English/Spanish), with no installation needed.
details:
What it does. Orbital is a 3D browser game where players design and fly NASA-style science missions. Each chapter starts with a real scientific question. Chapter 1 asks whether surface water extent changed between two dates (inspired by Landsat and SWOT). Chapter 2 asks which lunar sector has slopes safe for landing (Apollo 8 and LRO/LOLA). Chapter 3 asks how temperature changes between sunlit and shadowed spots on the Moon (LRO/Diviner and LCROSS). Mars chapters based on MRO and Perseverance at Jezero are planned.

How it works. In the workshop, players assemble a rocket from boosters, engines, tanks, antennas, power, memory and instruments. The game validates the design and shows Δv per stage. They launch with the keyboard, perform a gravity turn, stage and circularize. The physics includes gravity of the dominant body, atmosphere, heating, Max-Q, maneuver nodes, Earth–Moon patched conics and Kepler time warp that stops before critical events. In orbit, players fly over target zones, take measurements, store data and transmit it when a ground station or the deep-space network is in view and enough power is available. Each mission ends with a report that separates three things: the simulated measurement, its interpretation, and the result NASA actually published.

Benefits and impact. Orbital mechanics and mission science are usually taught with abstract equations or with simulators that are hard for beginners. Orbital teaches cause and effect through play. A 34-step guided tutorial explains apoapsis, periapsis, Δv, TWR, Max-Q, prograde, SAS and staging, and after two failures it offers an Assisted mode. Failing never costs progress, so players can experiment safely. The game is bilingual (Spanish/English) and runs in any desktop browser with no installation, so students and astronomy fans in Latin America and elsewhere can use it.

Tools. TypeScript, Three.js, Vite, HTML/CSS and HTML5 audio. Unit tests use the Node.js test runner, and an automated browser smoke test runs on Chrome or Edge. Every push deploys to GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions. There is no backend.

Creativity and design factors. Science is the only currency: there is no score and no budget per attempt. Assisted and manual flight use the same engines and the same propellant, so the assistant never cheats physics. Measuring and transmitting are separate steps, as they are on real missions. Simulated results are always labeled and never presented as NASA findings. The team also prioritized keyboard accessibility, visible focus, high contrast, support for reduced motion, and keeping the game playable after failure without losing progress.
